lead: Both readings are about faithful witness and the Lord who keeps those who belong to him. In the First Letter to Timothy, a young minister is told to fight the good fight of faith, holding to the confession he made, as Christ made his own good confession before Pilate. In John, at the winter feast of the Dedication, Jesus is pressed to say plainly whether he is the Messiah, and answers that his works already speak and that his sheep hear his voice. In the first week of Kaitha, the Church turns from the Apostles’ season to the long summer of ordinary discipleship: to hear the Shepherd’s voice, to follow, and to keep the faith to the end.

r.h: Fight the good fight of the faith
set: First Timothy is one of the Pastoral Letters, written to guide a young leader in the care of a church at Ephesus. The Church receives it as Scripture from the apostle Paul’s circle; it is traditionally attributed to Paul, while many scholars think a close disciple wrote it in his name after his death. The teaching is the same in either case.

The passage comes at the end of the letter, after warnings against love of money (6:3–10). “But as for you” turns from those false teachers to Timothy himself, and the letter closes with a solemn charge and a hymn of praise to God.
str: v. 11: flee what is wrong; pursue six virtues.
v. 12: fight the good fight; take hold of eternal life to which you were called.
vv. 13–14: a charge in the presence of God and of Christ, who made the good confession before Pilate: keep the commandment until the Lord appears.
vv. 15–16: praise of God, the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings, dwelling in unapproachable light.
kw: The picture is the athletic contest. Agōn gives our word “agony”; it can mean a race or a struggle. The faith is not only believed but striven for.
Open acknowledgement of faith, here probably made at Timothy’s baptism or ordination. Christ is the model: he also “made the good confession”.
The word the Pastoral Letters use for the coming of Christ, at his first coming and at the end. Timothy keeps the faith with that day in view.
vv: But as for you, man of God, shun all this; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
“Man of God” was the old title of Moses and the prophets. Timothy is named in their line. Shunning is only half the task; the other half is to pursue what is good.
Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life, to which you were called
Eternal life is both a gift already offered and a prize to be held fast. The Christian runs toward what has already been given.
In the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you
The name of Pilate is in the Creed because the Passion happened in real history. Christ’s confession before an earthly judge is the pattern for all who must give witness.
It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see;
The charge ends in worship. The God we serve is beyond all our seeing, and yet he has come near in Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ “bore witness to the truth” before Pilate, and that Christians are not to be ashamed of testifying to the Lord (CCC 2471). The Church has long read Paul’s picture of the good fight as the whole of the Christian life, with Baptism as the beginning of the contest. The hymn in verse 16 is used by the Fathers to teach that God cannot be seen by creatures unaided and is known only as he reveals himself (in substance; compare CCC 1028).

set: The festival of the Dedication (Hanukkah) remembered the re-dedication of the altar of the Temple in 164 BC under Judas Maccabeus, after the Temple had been profaned (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). It fell in winter, and John mentions the cold. Jesus walks in the portico of Solomon, a covered colonnade on the east side of the Temple.

This scene follows the Good Shepherd discourse earlier in the chapter (10:1–18). “The Jews” in John’s Gospel here means the leaders gathered round him, not the Jewish people; Jesus and all his first disciples were Jews. Their question is a real one, and he answers it.
str: vv. 22–23: the feast of the Dedication; Jesus in the portico of Solomon.
v. 24: the question: if you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.
vv. 25–26: his works in his Father’s name are his testimony; they do not believe because they are not of his flock.
vv. 27–28: the sheep hear, are known, follow, and receive eternal life; no one will snatch them from his hand.
kw: The festival that gives the passage its place and light. At the feast of the re-consecrated Temple, Jesus appears as the one in whom God truly dwells among his people.
In John, Jesus’ works are signs that reveal who he is and whose Son he is. The question “are you the Messiah?” has been answered by what he does, not only by what he says.
In John, to hear his voice means to listen and obey. The sheep recognise the Shepherd’s voice (10:3–4).
vv: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.”
They ask in the language of their hope. The difficulty is not that Jesus is silent but that his answer is not the kind they wanted: a Messiah who is also the Son of the Father.
Jesus answered, “I have told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name testify to me;
He points to his deeds. The same Jesus who speaks the Father’s words does the Father’s works.
My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
Three things mark the flock: they hear, he knows them, they follow. To be known by Christ comes first; it is his love that makes the following possible.
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand.
A promise of the Shepherd’s strength, not a licence for carelessness. We hold to it by hope and perseverance, listening to his voice each day.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church is the sheepfold whose gate is Christ, and the flock of which God himself is the shepherd (CCC 754). The promise that no one will snatch the sheep from his hand is read by the Church as a ground of hope: Christians hope for the grace of final perseverance, and ask it in prayer (CCC 2016). The Fathers read the works of Christ in this passage as testimony of his divinity: the Son who does the works of the Father is one with the Father, as the next verses say (10:30).

qa: If no one can snatch the sheep from Christ’s hand, can a Christian still be lost?

The promise is a true one: the Shepherd does not let go. The Church also teaches that we keep our own will and can turn from him by grave sin, and so we are called to keep faith and to ask for perseverance (CCC 2016). Hope in Christ’s hand and care for our own walk belong together, as in Timothy’s charge to fight the good fight.
study: Timothy is told to pursue six qualities: righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness. Which one do I most need this week, and what is one step I can take toward it?
Jesus says his sheep hear his voice. In what quiet place or moment of the day do I give him room to speak?
